I am trying to get away from Windows 7/ 10, and more into Linux. This particular laptop will just be used for music, movies, streaming, and PDF's when I game with friends.

I was looking at Mint, but wasn't sure the distro. I had used Ubuntu Gnome and KDE about 6 years ago, but that is the extent of my Linux knowledge.

Any suggestions for something that is basic and easy to learn that will run decently on this system?

EDIT: Update is located here https://voat.co/v/Linux/comments/1073126

Linux Mint Mate is what I run on my laptop and two desktops. It works like a champ and was very easy to learn.

It replaced Windows 7 on the laptop, by the way.

If you still need Windows 7 for some things, you can easily virtualize it using VirtualBox.
I'll second mint mate for a laptop of your specs. It's lightweight but can still do games and multimedia.

People here love mint, and I don't. It just didn't feel how I wanted it to. I have nothing against it, but it's not for me, and if you're not liking what you see of it, then I'd suggest looking at others.

Right now I run OpenSuse LEAP with GNOME on my laptop as a work machine, but I can use it as an entertainment center just as easily. It comes with some good stuff out of the box, and it keeps itself up to date really nicely.

Oh, and if your linux knowledge is from 6 years ago, don't listen to the Arch fans just yet. It takes a ton of work to get it running, and it sounds like you will have a really bad time with it. Arch is the complete opposite of "basic and easy to learn."
The architect project is a great way to get arch with a graphical installer. Still have some tweaking to do after but it's a great way to get things going.

There are three things that I absolutely dislike about mint:

  1. They try to club in each and every software including adobe flash and chrome into their repository. I'm not an overly huge FOSS fanatic, but I prefer to use open source tech wherever I can.
  2. They try to imitate the Windows OS by giving a start menu and all. This ends up giving a crappy desktop and poor impression of linux.
  3. The recent fiasco where their website got hacked and a number of compromised copies were downloaded. I'd have considered changing my views if the mint community had shown that they have taken pro-active measures towards security, but unfortunately they haven't.

I was a big fan of Mint, then I tried Manjaro and now I'm a bigger fan of Manjaro. Among other things I've got it running on an old Dell laptop with an Atom CPU and something like 1MB of RAM. Runs soother than Mint did.

It's whatever the default was when I installed it -- the laptop is not with me right now and I can't recall.

Otherwise I'm running KDE Plasma 5 which is fantastic, but granted it's on heavier machines. I'm not familiar with AMD CPUs so I don't know how yours is rated but since you can install multiple DEs and then choose which one to run there's no reason not to check out a variety.

I use Arch currently but would not suggest it or it's derivitives for new people. Mint with Cinnimon I would say is the definitive best answer.

Manjaro is Arch for begineers but when you want to start doing more technical stuff you should have a system that will hold your hand a little bit more. Not so much the system as online documents and that's why you should use a debian/ubuntu/mint varient hands down.

New people should stay in that ecosystem for at least a few years just so online guides are always relevent. You will grow the most and quickest with that system and then when you platue you can switch to Arch.

You will like cinnamon more and your system can easily handle it. Mine is currently only using 22MB of memory and 0% cpu. Your computer is bigger than mine. Human factors are more critical than machine factors.
Linux mint Debian edition. Mate version. Very, very easy to use.

A laptop like that should have no problems running Mint crisply. Something with less power and I'd recommend looking into Xubuntu, Bodhi or other OS. Get a usb drive and a distro installer and boot up several recommended distros and see what you think.
I've been using Ubuntu since 2011 and recently switched to Xubuntu and I'll recommend you to use either of them. But please go for the LTS version (1604) if you want a stable experience.
